The post Review: 2023 One Stone Cabernet Sauvignon Paso Robles appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Ancient Peaks offshoot One Stone continues to surprise with its ultra-value wines.

The 2023 edition of this screw-capped cabernet defies expectations, offering moderated sweetness and varietal authenticity, notes of currants tempered with oak, rhubarb, and a dash of vanilla, finishing with a touch of spicy licorice. Notes of nutmeg cling to the finish, which echoes the gently tannic currants visible from the start, eventually followed by touches of dark chocolate. It’s all quite gentle and approachable from start to finish, less earthy than the 2021 bottling and more immediately approachable — great in its own, different way. Seems like a fine way to go at things to me.

Again, a great value.

A- / $20

title: Review: Powers Irish Rye
summary:

As the name suggests, this is a 100% rye whiskey, column distilled at Midleton and aged for 4 to 5 years in a mix of virgin American oak, first-fill, and…

The post Review: Powers Irish Rye appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
While Irish whiskey is typically crafted from a blend of grains — predominantly barley — with this bottling Powers takes things in an unusual direction. As the name suggests, this is a 100% rye whiskey, column distilled at Midleton and aged for 4 to 5 years in a mix of virgin American oak, first-fill, and second-fill casks.

Let’s dig in.

Powers Irish Rye Review

This whiskey is immediately interesting for the way it effectively blends the styles of a classic Irish whiskey with a spicy, American style rye. The nose is quite hearty, in contrast to the often wispy, ephemeral Irish style, a mix of bracing herbs, sweeter baking spice, and honeyed cereal grains all hit the nose together. There’s also more of a pure wood influence here than in a traditional Irish, with notes of almond and apple wood lingering with time in glass.

The palate does not change the script much, kicking off with notes of almond and sesame, then a layer of melon, more cantaloupe than honeydew. The whiskey turns rather grassy from that point, quite fresh with overtones of lemon and bright baking spices. Notes of pastry cream infused with cinnamon offer a boldly dessert-like midpalate, though the sweetness is moderated. The experience oscillates — some herbaceousness, some sweeter tones, then back again — until it lands on the finish with the essence of almond croissants.

All told, it’s a wholly atypical Irish whiskey — and, perhaps, all the better for it.

86.4 proof.

A- / $35 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Waterdrop Instant Hot and Cold Countertop Water Filter Dispenser CT01
summary:
Isn’t it about high time we had space-saving on-demand convenience for fetching filtered hot or cold water at home with a touch of a button? Hadn’t thought of it? Probably not top of mind given the existing options in the water category. Refrigerators come with spouts for cold water, and electric kettles boil water in…

The post Review: Waterdrop Instant Hot and Cold Countertop Water Filter Dispenser CT01 appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Isn’t it about high time we had space-saving on-demand convenience for fetching filtered hot or cold water at home with a touch of a button? Hadn’t thought of it? Probably not top of mind given the existing options in the water category. Refrigerators come with spouts for cold water, and electric kettles boil water in under a minute with a push of a button, so there’s no shortage of gadgets that attach to your faucet for filtration. But, indeed, the time has come for a standalone all-in-one countertop unit to continue to narrow that convenience gap. 

Let’s consider today’s candidate from Waterdrop, well regarded for their filtration systems, who now offers the CT01 Instant Hot & Cold Countertop Water Filter System. It weighs about 15 lbs, stands 14.44″ × 10.61″ × 13.43 with a detachable 1.32 gallon tank to forego plumbing installation and just plugs into any outlet of your choice. (We’re no strangers to countertop filtration systems or Waterdrop, see our 2025 review of their reverse osmosis filter dispenser.)

The device applies an “Advanced 6-Stage Filtration System” that “reduces chlorine, rust, and other impurities while retaining beneficial minerals like calcium and magnesium.” You get hot or cold water “in seconds” with just a touch of various buttons offering personalized control and customization of temperature and volume. The 1.32-gallon container holds the equivalent of “28 × 6 oz cups” or in more relatable everyday metrics, about 6 to 10 commonly sized refillable water bottles. 

One can’t consider convenience without considering setup and maintenance, and, especially when it comes to “smart” things, how immune they are to user error. On balance, you only need to plug this into the wall to operate; it does not require plumbing to attach to your faucet or pipes. Which means the water supply is wholly dependent on you filling it up. It’s a decent trade off in my mind. 

The “touch-button” proposition is a bit more nuanced. Yes, you just have to press a couple of shiny little icons to fill your cup. But those shiny little icons need introductions about what they do and more critically, what you should not do. As a re-emerging luddite that admits knobs and dials are increasingly more appealing, trying to decipher how to manage the cute little figures in the proper order took embarrassingly longer than I care to admit. I was nervous a careless swipe would lead to water all over the floor or a malfunction. I took time to read the manual, and when I still didn’t trust myself, I checked the website to reach customer support. I was happy to see they had a Chat option, and was disappointed when no chat person or bot was home. I switched to old fashioned email to customer service. Unfortunately I am still waiting for a response, but with some steady pacing and careful repeat studying of the manual, I managed to figure out what the various icons were and what it means when one of them flashes or disappears. 

Post-testing inertia has left this temporary unit somewhat semi-permanently situated on our countertop. Increasingly our household has become spoiled with shaving minutes/seconds of the day to access instant hot or cold water. I knew I was a convert when I went to turn on our electric kettle and thought: Wait, there is already hot water just a few feet away, right now. I placed a mug with a tea bag under the dispenser and touched a few little pictures and walked away while the process completed. 

The long and short of it is that the product delivers on its promises. Water is clean tasting (an oxymoronic assessment, I know), and the convenience is all there. And it’s all packaged in a very sleek contraption to boot (think Eve from Wall-E). The filter lasts through 300 gallons before replacement is needed, though note that both the side and lower tanks are recommended to be emptied every few days. That is a chore I can definitely handle.  

A- / $220 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

title: Review: New Riff Wheated Bourbon 6 Years Old
summary:
Based in Newport, Kentucky — just a stone’s throw from the Ohio River, and right across from Cincinnati — New Riff has never been averse to playing with mash bills and grain types. Its latest special release whiskey honors that ethos, delivering a wheated bourbon from a notably uncommon recipe: 65% corn 18% floor-malted wheat…

The post Review: New Riff Wheated Bourbon 6 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Based in Newport, Kentucky — just a stone’s throw from the Ohio River, and right across from Cincinnati — New Riff has never been averse to playing with mash bills and grain types. Its latest special release whiskey honors that ethos, delivering a wheated bourbon from a notably uncommon recipe:

  • 65% corn
  • 18% floor-malted wheat
  • 10% unmalted wheat
  • 7% dark wheat

According to a distillery representative, that grain bill takes inspiration from beer and allowed production staff to flex their deep brewing experience. New Riff is no stranger to beer-inspired whiskeys, also exemplified by a relatively recent “Duet” collab with Rhinegeist Brewery.

This new wheated bourbon was made from the aforementioned mash bill, then aged for six years. It’s presented as a bottled-in-bond product and — as with virtually all New Riff whiskeys — is presented without chill filtration. But getting your hands on a bottle may require jumping through a few minor hoops. This bottling is the newest product exclusive to New Riff’s Whiskey Club. It’s free to join, though releases are available for distillery pickup only.

Let’s see how it tastes.

New Riff Wheated Bourbon 6 Years Old Review

The nose starts off with ample candied fruit, specifically lemon drops and watermelon Jolly Rancher. At first, it’s bright and slightly tart, though aromas get richer, sweeter, oakier, and more grain-forward with a bit more time in the glass. (Yes, it evolves quite a bit!) Malt syrup and saltwater taffy are up next, followed by Weetabix cereal, which together bring a lightly sweet grain quality where the wheat really punches through in several forms. Those early fruit candy notes are almost gone after a few minutes, replaced (it seems) by lemongrass. Cocoa powder and cinnamon round out a nose that feels adjacent to New Riff’s classic bourbon profile with a touch more grain.

Even for a standard bottled-in-bond, this hits first as an easy sipper, drinking noticeably below proof. That’s not necessarily a knock against. Indeed, that first taste is lovely, like a fusion of those lemon drops and the milk leftover from a bowl of Cracklin’ Oat Bran. Toasted grain and more sweet citrus accumulate toward the midpalate, like charred sourdough bread topped with orange marmalade or apricot jam. It’s a pleasant combo at this point, though a somewhat thin mouthfeel allows the fruit to die back early while bread remains, contributing to a nearly charred character. Flavors continue on their gradually more tannic route, and for six years old, the back palate becomes fairly heavy on leather. The finish layers on most zested citrus, cereal grain, and oak with a smaller thread of lingering sweet breakfast cereal.

100 proof.

B+ / $60

The post Review: La Pulga Tequila (Updated 2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Tequila continues to take the country by storm but perhaps nowhere more so than in Texas. Three Ft. Worth-based entrepreneurs are getting in on the action with another addition to the growing La Pulga, a tequila distilled and bottled in Jalisco, Mexico but proudly born in “Cowtown.” Or so goes the press release. The name comes from the La Pulga market, one of the oldest open air flea markets in the country and a fixture of Ft. Worth. Notably, the company’s Head of Spirits is Ale Ochoa, a whiskey scientist and Master Blender formerly with Fort Worth-based Firestone & Robertson Distilling Co. Today, we’re looking at two of the brand’s three classic expressions, each of which is distilled from 100% Blue Weber agave and certified additive-free.

Update 2026: We’re adding coverage of La Pulga’s Double Barrel Reposado.

NOM 1068.

La Pulga Tequila Blanco Review

This unaged silver tequila is impressively earthy and green on the nose with big notes of olive brine, clay, and cut grass. As it opens, agave pulp, lime peel, and plantain add some sweetness, but a healthy dash of black pepper keeps things on the savory side. The palate is a touch sweeter than the aroma but still quite rustic and piquant with a rich minerality – sea salt and flint – and notes of fresh agave, dried lime, and cilantro. The finish is peppery and dry with lingering notes of green olive and citrus. 80 proof. B+ / $45 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

La Pulga Tequila Reposado Review

Seven months of aging in ex-bourbon barrels has really subdued the blanco’s aroma, silencing for the most part all of those green and briny notes with a soft, subtle blanket of vanilla icing and cinnamon sugar. As it opens, the agave, classically vegetal and sweet, emerges. The palate is more viscous than the blanco with comparatively lush notes of cinnamon syrup, honey candies, and cooked agave. While sweeter than the blanco, it’s still well-balanced. The midpalate, nicely spiced with clove, cracked pepper, and grated cinnamon, transitions seamlessly to a warming, balanced finish of Red Hots, wintergreen, and vanilla taffy. While the blanco is a bit more interesting, the reposado should be a crowd pleaser. 80 proof. A- / $55 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

La Pulga Tequila Reposado Double Barrel Review

This limited edition reposado takes the standard La Pulga reposado (as above) and gives it a second maturation in fresh Still Austin Red Corn Bourbon barrels. There’s no word on the length of the finishing, but the tequila is bottled at a higher abv, 45%. It’s been several years since I’ve tasted La Pulga’s standard Reposado, but this expression is quite a lively experience and, based on my earlier notes, a significant upgrade. Seductive and rich on the nose, the tequila pops right away with vanilla and cinnamon notes, the underlying agave character an exercise in gentle restraint. Above all, it smells clean and refreshing, immediately inviting. On the palate a rush of vanilla caramel kicks things off, backed up with some bright citrus, almost juicy with orange notes. Baking spice follows but it remains quite gentle, gingery and laced with allspice, complementary to the sweeter notes that kick things off. A final rush of agave reminds you that you’re drinking tequila, not rum, leaving things on a gentle, grassy note. The best I’ve seen from La Pulga to date. 90 proof. A / $70

The post Review: Sapporo Premium Non-Alcoholic Beer appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Also known as Sapporo 0.0%, Sapporo Premium Non-Alcoholic is the N/A version of the Japanese classic, more or less anyway. Unlike a lot of non-alc beers, it doesn’t particularly taste like classic Sapporo, attacking with a very lemon-forward quality that threatens to overwhelm everything before it ever gets going. A spritz of apple cider adds a sweeter fruit element, helping to calm things down at least a little. As the palate develops the beer takes on a distinct maltiness, tempering the earlier fruit notes. Some brown sugar lingers underneath all the grainy notes until a reprise of that zippy lemon returns in time for the finish. It’s certainly a pleasant enough brew, though it feels like the point of all that bright acidity is to cover up the lack of alcohol. Weirdly enough, it works.

B+ / $11 per six-pack

Rather, it’s a 5 year old American single malt…

The post Review: Dogfish Head Distilling x Rolling Stone American Single Malt Whiskey appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Dogfish Head‘s distilling arm continues its growth with this odd collaboration, produced in collaboration with Rolling Stone magazine. (Mind the distinction: The Rolling Stones, the band, have their own collab with Jose Cuervo.)

As is the norm for Dogfish Head, this isn’t some boring old sourced whiskey. Rather, it’s a 5 year old American single malt that is matured in 12 different cask types, including Dogfish Head refill whiskey barrels, brandy casks, and Samuel Adams Utopias beer barrels. It’s only available in Delaware, New York, New Jersey, Maryland, Washington D.C., and Massachusetts, and in limited quantities, so if the below review sounds appealing, hop on it.

Dogfish Head Distilling x Rolling Stone American Single Malt Whiskey Review

American single malt can often come across as underdeveloped, but this five year old feels like it has made some remarkable progression. While it could stand a few more years in the barrel(s), there’s ample nuance here that’s worth investigating.

The nose is as complex as anything matured in 12 barrel types could and should be. It’s quite grainy at first blush, and time in glass narrows the aromatic focus to the influence of wood. But traditional lumberyard and sawdust elements aren’t the play here: Notes of peach wood and apple wood, laced with gentle fruitiness, are surprisingly heady, alongside lighter but persistent aromas of floral incense and toasted spices.

The palate hits with a gentler cereal tone, but with more exotic elements close behind: toasted coconut, sherry-soaked citrus peel, and peppery hops all swirled into a core of cookie batter, part sugar, part gingerbread. Mildly but increasingly smoky as it develops on the palate, the whiskey drops some of its sweeter elements to allow a more savory character to develop on the finish, baked apple meandering toward red apple skins and back to apple wood. In the end, hints of tobacco ring the edges — if that ain’t rock ‘n’ roll, I don’t know what is.

90 proof.

B+ / $70

title: Review: Coors Whiskey Blended American Malt 8 Years Old
summary:
It’s unclear if the brand is dropping its old Five Trail and Barmen 1873 monikers, but Golden, Colorado’s iconic Coors beer brand continues to ramp up its distilling arm, now releasing products under what seems like a wholly obvious name: Coors Whiskey Co. Coors Whiskey Co. Blended American Malt Whiskey is an 8 year old…

The post Review: Coors Whiskey Blended American Malt 8 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
It’s unclear if the brand is dropping its old Five Trail and Barmen 1873 monikers, but Golden, Colorado’s iconic Coors beer brand continues to ramp up its distilling arm, now releasing products under what seems like a wholly obvious name: Coors Whiskey Co.

Coors Whiskey Co. Blended American Malt Whiskey is an 8 year old malt whiskey — not an American Single Malt but rather a blend, as it’s made with whiskey produced with Coors’ own proprietary malt as well as other Colorado malt whiskeys.

“Most whiskey stories begin in the barrel. Ours begins with the grain,” said Susie McInerney, Sr. Marketing Manager, Coors Spirits Co. “Malt has been part of the Coors story since the earliest days of the company, rooted in long-standing malting tradition. This release represents a natural evolution for Coors Whiskey Co. and is proof that what goes into our whiskey—down to the grain—makes all the difference, and creates something truly differentiated in the category.”

Let’s put down the bottle of Banquet and give it a whirl.

Coors Whiskey Blended American Malt 8 Years Old Review

The nose is a huge surprise — boldly malty, to be sure, but also smoky and quite sharp, far rougher around the edges than the typical malt whiskey (no matter what country it’s from). While quite buttery and heavy with spice, particularly cinnamon, the apparently aggressive char level is what threatens to overwhelm things from the jump.

The palate comes across as old and austere, surprisingly past its prime with its combination of torched citrus peel, sooty creosote, and a lightly industrial quality atop it all. Is this a sherried whiskey? If so, the influence has gone a bit off the rails, washing out the delicacy of the malt and leaving behind a pungency that simply never quits. I suppose some drinkers may gravitate to this level of face bashing, but I found it mostly off-putting, save for some more pleasant moments of milder orange and apricot that eventually peek out on the finish.

I spent two days tasting this whiskey, trying to coax out some of the (many) tasting notes that Coors outlines in its press material, and while there’s fruit (pear, namely) somewhere in the mix, it’s buried so deeply by all the char and smoke as to be largely inscrutable.

110.5 proof.

B- / $80

title: Review: Bourbon de Luxe 7 Years Old Rum Cask Finish and 8 Years Old
summary:
Some bourbon brands are born in the distillery. Others are born in the marketplace, shaped by the people who sell them, the companies that carry them forward, and the circumstances that determine whether they survive. Bourbon de Luxe belongs to the latter category, and its story stretches back more than a century, through Prohibition, the…

The post Review: Bourbon de Luxe 7 Years Old Rum Cask Finish and 8 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Some bourbon brands are born in the distillery. Others are born in the marketplace, shaped by the people who sell them, the companies that carry them forward, and the circumstances that determine whether they survive. Bourbon de Luxe belongs to the latter category, and its story stretches back more than a century, through Prohibition, the rise of some of Kentucky’s most influential whiskey companies, and an eventual disappearance from store shelves.

The brand traces its roots to 1911, when Fort Worth, Texas, whiskey merchant Milton Eppstein introduced Bourbon de Luxe to a growing American whiskey market. The timing was significant. Just nine years later, Prohibition would bring legal whiskey production and sales to an abrupt halt across much of the country. Yet Bourbon de Luxe would prove more resilient than many of its contemporaries. In 1926, Kentucky’s R.E. Wathen Co. acquired the brand, and it subsequently became part of American Medicinal Spirits, one of the companies authorized to sell whiskey for medicinal purposes during Prohibition. In an era when whiskey brands faced an uncertain future, that distinction helped keep the name alive.

The next chapter placed Bourbon de Luxe among considerably bigger players. In 1929, American Medicinal Spirits became part of National Distillers, a major force in American whiskey whose portfolio included such established names as Old Grand-Dad, Old Crow, and Old Taylor. Bourbon de Luxe remained in that corporate lineage when National Distillers sold its brands to Jim Beam in 1987. Production continued for years afterward, but by the early 2000s, Bourbon de Luxe had largely disappeared from the market.

For a brand with roots in the pre-Prohibition era, that might have been the end of the story. Instead, its next chapter would bring it back to a family with a connection to its past.

In December 2023, Turner Wathen and Jordan Morris secured the Bourbon de Luxe trademark, setting the stage for its eventual return in 2024. The pair had built Rolling Fork Spirits around an appreciation for carefully selected, blended, and finished spirits, establishing a reputation through their work with rum. But bourbon had always been part of the plan, provided they could find the right brand and whiskey to justify bringing it back. For Wathen, the opportunity carried an additional layer of meaning: his family had been involved in the American whiskey business for generations, and Bourbon de Luxe was among the brands associated with that legacy.

The revival was not simply a matter of putting a familiar name on a bottle. Wathen and Morris wanted the whiskey behind the label to merit its return, choosing to launch Bourbon de Luxe as a Kentucky straight bourbon rather than relying on nostalgia alone. Their first release arrived in 2024, reintroducing a name that had been absent from shelves for more than two decades. In 2026, Bourbon de Luxe released a small batch bourbon aged for 8 years and a small batch bourbon aged for 7 years finished in Rolling Fork Rum barrels.

And so Bourbon de Luxe finds itself in a familiar yet distinctly modern position: an old name in a new chapter of American whiskey, carrying the history of the businesses and people that kept it alive while attempting to establish its own identity for a new generation of bourbon drinkers. More than a century after its introduction, the label has returned, but its latest chapter must be judged on what is in the bottle, not merely what is printed on it.

Bourbon de Luxe Rum Cask Finished Bourbon 7 Years Old Review

Batch 2026-02 combines six barrels coopered by Independent Stave Company and filled before October 2017. Two barrels originated at Bardstown Bourbon Company, distilled from 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley. These barrels spent more than two years finishing in Rolling Fork Lost Rum Cask Series barrels. One finishing cask previously held Worthy Park rum for 18 years, while the other held Trinidadian 10 Cane rum for 17 years. The bourbon entered these casks in August 2024.

The remaining four barrels were distilled at Green River in Owensboro, Kentucky, from 70% corn, 21% rye, and 9% malted barley. These barrels spent nearly 14 months finishing in Rolling Fork Wheated Cask Wonder Rum casks, with the bourbon entering the rum casks in July 2025.

All bourbon entered the rum casks between 119 and 124 proof. Before finishing, the youngest bourbon had aged for seven years and one month, while the oldest had reached seven years and 10 months, giving the blend an average age of seven years and four months. All barrels were dumped for blending in August 2026 at a natural harvest proof of 119.

The rum cask influence announces itself immediately on the nose, led by a pronounced turbinado sugar aroma. Bright orange zest follows, adding a citrus edge before banana peel takes a prominent position. Nutmeg joins the mix, accompanied by a faint trace of mint. The result brings bourbon and rum together in a way that makes sense, allowing the finishing casks to make their presence known without obscuring the underlying whiskey.

The palate starts with a pronounced dose of spice, as clove and black pepper take the lead. Through the mid-palate, the rum influence becomes more apparent with unsweetened dried pineapple and burnt orange peel appearing alongside a dry mouthfeel. That dryness intensifies toward the finish, where cocoa powder and spicy cinnamon join leather and another dose of black pepper.

This is a well-executed rum cask-finished bourbon that drinks as though it spent several additional years in the barrel. Those who find rum finishes overly sweet should take particular interest here. The rum influence is readily apparent, but it shares the glass with plenty of spice, dry citrus, and earthy notes. Rather than relying on sugar-driven flavors to make its point, Batch 2026-02 offers a more savory, spice-forward take on rum cask finishing. 111 proof. A- / $65

Bourbon de Luxe Bourbon 8 Years Old Review

Batch 2026-01 brings together 15 barrels from two Kentucky distilleries, with two different mashbills contributing to the final blend. Three barrels were distilled at Green River in Owensboro, Kentucky, from a mashbill of 75% corn, 21% rye, and 4% malted barley. The remaining 12 barrels came from Bardstown Bourbon Company, distilled from 60% corn, 36% rye, and 4% malted barley. All 15 barrels received a #3 char and matured for at least eight years before being dumped for blending in June 2026.

The nose opens with buttery toffee and sweet, waxy honeycomb. Orange sherbet follows, delivering the citrus flavor of orange without the sharp bite of fresh zest. French toast rounds things out, bringing bready notes of egg wash, cinnamon, and nutmeg, minus the maple syrup.

The palate begins with the combination of caramel and apple found in a caramel apple from the county fair, followed by Honey Nut Cheerios. Through the mid-palate, Little Debbie Oatmeal Cream Pies and candied ginger enter the picture. Sweetness, baked grain, and spice work together particularly well here, accompanied by an exceptionally oily mouthfeel.

The finish takes a different route, moving away from the sweeter opening and placing greater emphasis on spice. Cinnamon chewing gum and grapefruit provide the first wave of flavor, followed by black pepper and an almost effervescent burst of cherry Pop Rocks.

This is an excellent bourbon from the first sip through the finish. What stands out most is the progression of flavors, with each stage offering something different rather than repeating the same notes throughout. The movement from dessert-like sweetness to potent spice gives the bourbon plenty of appeal, while the quality of the blend makes the price especially attractive. Considering both its age and what it delivers in the glass, Batch 2026-01 could rank among the best bourbon values of 2026. 124.5 proof. A / $65 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

The post Review: Wines of Iterum, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Joe Dobbes is an icon in Oregon’s Willamette Valley, whose wineries Dobbes Family Estate and Wine by Joe have been staples of the region for decades. Iterum is Dobbes’s self-proclaimed “retirement project,” a prestige brand founded in 2019 that draws on Dobbes’s deep knowledge of Oregon terroir and features numerous single vineyard expressions in its arsenal.

The bottles are quirky — they don’t even note the varietal on the front label — but that only adds to their significant charm.

Thoughts on four new releases follow. 2022 is the current vintage for most of these wines.

2024 Iterum Estate Sauvignon Blanc Orchard House Vineyard – Remarkably expressive for sauvignon blanc (though not an iconic offering from Willamette), this is a fruit-forward expression of a classic style, with upfront notes of apricot and peach layered with saline and, later, coconut cream, chased by lemon curd. The lattermost of these offers a decidedly tart character to the finish, though the lemon meringue pie quality finds a tempering note in late-arriving notes of crushed graham crackers and some toasted coconut. Dessert is served. A- / $50

2022 Iterum Estate Chardonnay Orchard House Vineyard – The pale straw color of this wine is misleading, as it’s a fairly classically structured chardonnay, though the oak and vanilla are kept in check by terraced layers of lemon peel, grapefruit, and mild notes of guava. The body is rich and exotic, and it would evoke the best wedding cake you’d ever had if there was more sugar in the mix, but fortunately there’s not. Instead, a bright acidity brings the finish to a slightly salty crescendo, with echoes of lemon, almond, and orchids draped around the neck. A- / $75

2022 Iterum Estate Pinot Noir “Old Friend” Quailhurst – This Chehalem Mountains AVA bottling surprised right away with its boldly earthy attack, gravelly and almost muddy, any sense of fruit requiring a lengthy spell in glass before it reveals itself. When it does, dried cherries and prunes force their way forward to eventually dominate, layered with dark chocolate, graphite, and ashy creosote. The experience remains heady, almost overwhelming, the weight of its massive body a leaden twist on the pinot formula. Time in glass helps loosen the threads a bit, but this takes a significant amount of patience. B / $90

2022 Iterum Estate Pinot Noir “Old Friend” Symonette Vineyard – A vibrant and far different pinot than the Quailhurst bottling, this Eola-Amity Hills expression is a lithe expression of Oregon pinot noir at its very best: Bright cherry fruit, layered with both raspberry and strawberry, is chased by soothing notes of black tea, followed by the lightest dusting of crushed slate and powdered anise. The earthier notes complement a lively fruit attack, the finish finding a deft balance between the two halves, concluding with an echo of fruit tea, ever so slightly exuding a minerally dust. It goes on and on forever, back and forth, back and forth. One of my favorite pinots in recent memory, I love this stuff. A / $90
